title: Language Model Enabled Structure Prediction from Infrared Spectra of Mixtures
experiments_summary: The study employed the following experiments and methods: (1) Synthetic mixture spectrum generation: IR spectra of binary mixtures were synthesized by linearly combining pure compound spectra weighted by fractional concentrations, formally defined as a weighted sum of component spectra. (2) Experimental validation of linear combination assumption: ATR-IR spectra of four pure compounds (Cyclohexylamine, N,N-Dimethylethylenediamine, 4-Chloronitrobenzene, and a fourth compound) and their binary mixtures—both balanced and unbalanced—were measured in the lab and compared against synthetically generated mixture spectra. Additionally, mixtures of Cyclohexanecarboxylic acid and diethylene glycol monobutyl ether were measured for balanced and unbalanced binary cases. MAE between synthetic and experimental spectra was computed and contextualized against Gaussian noise levels. (3) Model architecture: An encoder-decoder Transformer was extended from Alberts et al., using patch-based IR spectrum embedding (patch size 150 cm⁻¹), text tokenization of molecular formulae and concentrations, and SMILES tokenization for output. The input prompt format was: MOLECULAR FORMULA | % CONCENTRATION | MIXTURE SPECTRUM → SMILES. (4) Spectral alignment network ablation: A reconstruction module was added to encourage encoder representations specific to the target component. Two architectures (CNN and MLP) were tested in combination with two loss functions (MAE and MSE), and the weighting hyperparameter λ was varied across values {1, 5, 50}. All configurations were evaluated on binary balanced (50/50) mixtures using simulated spectra. (5) Two-stage training: Models were pretrained on ~790,000 simulated IR spectra from Alberts et al. (GAFF force field molecular dynamics), then fine-tuned on the NIST gas-phase IR database (3,453 compounds, 6–13 heavy atoms). Five-fold cross-validation was used during fine-tuning. (6) Imbalanced mixture experiments: Models were trained and evaluated on binary mixtures with ratios 50/50, 40/60, 30/70, 20/80, and 10/90. A multitask learning approach trained a single model simultaneously on all composition ratios. Ablation studies compared single-task versus multitask models. The best-performing alignment configuration (CNN, MAE, λ=50) was applied to all imbalanced datasets. (7) Ternary mixture experiments: The same modeling approach was extended to ternary balanced mixtures using NIST database spectra. (8) Experimental validation on real mixtures: 15 binary mixtures were measured using ATR-IR spectroscopy and evaluated using the multitask model trained on gas-phase synthetic mixture spectra. A rejection sampling post-processing strategy was applied to discard invalid SMILES or formula-inconsistent predictions. (9) Evaluation metrics used throughout: Top-1, Top-5, and Top-10 accuracy (percentage of correctly predicted molecules within top-n candidates) and mean Tanimoto similarity between Top-1 prediction and ground truth.
